clue.text: Actor playing on any screen

indicators.note: letters that are playing are frolicking about, so the words that follow are rearranged

parts.note: the eleven letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A film star appearing on whichever screen you happen to be watching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' looks like it describes the actor's role, but it signals the rearrangement of the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish star famous as the first James Bond on film is a well-known screen performer.

clue.text: Scoundrel hosting oddly dull do

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the first word holds the next piece within it

parts.note: a swine is a contemptible person

indicators.note: oddly keeps the letters in odd-numbered positions of the next word

parts.note: first and third letters of dull

explanation.surface: A rogue throws a boring party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like a party, the way the surface uses it, but here it is the verb meaning to cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone is informal British slang for cheating or conning them out of something.

clue.text: Silly sailors for all to see on road

parts.note: AB is an able seaman, so sailors are ABS
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing
RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: Foolish seamen making a public spectacle of themselves in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film rating meaning suitable for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something absurd is ridiculous or foolish, a straightforward synonym for silly behaviour or ideas.

clue.text: Fruit, peanut and cola mixed together

indicators.note: mixing things together scrambles them, so the letters of both words are combined and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A snack recipe: fruit with peanuts and fizzy cola stirred in.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantaloupe is a variety of melon with orange flesh, so it is one kind of fruit.

clue.text: New physio regularly turned up for something to eat

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means the letters read from bottom to top
regularly means at even intervals, taking every second letter of the word

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of physio

explanation.surface: A new physiotherapist arrived with a snack.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is informal British slang for food or a meal, so it is something you eat.

clue.text: Agent wasted year framing young girl

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so the scrambled letters go round the next piece
something wasted is wrecked or ruined, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written
a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A spy squandered twelve months setting up a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is someone sent on a mission to represent another, so an agent or envoy.

clue.text: Golly! EU getting reformed may be what's on the table in winter

definitions.text: may be what's on the table in winter

indicators.note: something reformed has been reshaped, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Surprise that the European Union is being reformed, changing what we eat at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed' seems to be about EU politics, but it shuffles all seven letters of the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A yule log is a chocolate sponge roll decorated like a log, served as a Christmas dessert in winter.

clue.text: Offender, young man, seeing red?

parts.note: crim is a short informal word for a criminal
a son is a young male relative

explanation.surface: A young criminal is getting angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeing red' reads as losing one's temper; only red is the definition, with seeing as the joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimson is a deep shade of red, so it is a colour within that family.

clue.text: "Winning daily is dull," I claim initially

parts.note: a daily is a cleaning woman, also called a char
taken as written
mat (or matt) describes a dull finish without shine
taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: first letter of claim

explanation.surface: Someone claims that winning every day has become boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like an adverb, but it is the British noun for a cleaner who comes in each day, also called a char.
explanation.definitionFit: A winning personality is attractive and appealing, which is what a charismatic one is too.

clue.text: Almost dead — perhaps Dennis suffocates!

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a stiff is slang for a corpse; as an adjective, stiff can mean dead
Les Dennis is a British comedian and game show host, so Dennis suggests LES

explanation.surface: A dramatic claim that someone is nearly done for because a man called Dennis is choking them.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Dennis is a British entertainer who hosted the TV quiz Family Fortunes; the clue uses his surname to point to his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: To stifle someone is to deprive them of air, which is a synonym for smothering or choking.

clue.text: State one blunder in first auction?

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: the first auction in a series could be called sale one
the Roman numeral for one
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: Admitting a mistake at the very first sale, with a question mark hinting at whimsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First auction' is read playfully as SALE ONE, and the question mark flags that liberty; I and ERR go in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sierra Leone is a country in West Africa, and a country can be called a state.

clue.text: Criminal alarmed new official

indicators.note: something criminal is wrong or crooked, so the letters are bent out of their order

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A crook frightened the newly appointed officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun, the crook in the story, but it is the adjective telling you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An alderman is a member of a town or city council, holding civic office.

clue.text: Legendary lover's confession from dealer?

parts.note: an admission of a sale: 'I sold'
a drug dealer's goods could be E, slang for ecstasy

explanation.surface: A famous romantic figure admits something a trader might say.
explanation.walkthrough: The dealer confesses 'I sold E', E being slang for the drug ecstasy. Isolde loved Tristan in the medieval legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolde is the heroine of the Tristan legend, famed for her doomed romance with the knight Tristan.

clue.text: Place to buy a jumper?

parts.note: surface reading: a shop selling knitted sweaters, which the British call jumpers; setter's reading: a jumper is an insect that leaps, so you would buy it at a market named after that bug

explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is a British word for a sweater, which is the picture; a flea is a famous jumper, and the term means a second-hand street market.
explanation.definitionFit: A flea market is an outdoor market selling cheap second-hand goods, including old clothes such as sweaters.

clue.text: Belief kids fear outsiders? The opposite!

indicators.note: the opposite of outer letters is inner ones, so only the middle of each word is kept

parts.note: the inside two letters of kids
the inside two letters of fear

explanation.surface: A notion that children are scared of strangers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outsiders' first suggests taking the first and last letters, but 'the opposite' flips that to the insides.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea can be an opinion or conviction someone holds, a looser synonym for belief.

clue.text: Standard outing, I understand

parts.note: a jolly is a British informal word for a fun trip or jaunt
radio slang meaning message received and understood

explanation.surface: Someone acknowledging that a normal trip is planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' looks like an adjective meaning normal, but it is a flag; a jolly is a British word for a pleasure trip.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull-and-crossbones pirate flag is a banner, and a standard is another word for a flag.

clue.text: Telling mum?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the act of narrating or recounting a story
second meaning: a mother is a family member

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests passing a secret to your mother; 'mum' could also mean silent, but here it is the mother herself.
explanation.definitionFit: A relation is both an account given of events and a family member such as a mother.

clue.text: Long-term strategy: smear chap for Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: smear is plaster and chap is man; swap their initial sounds

explanation.surface: A grand scheme described as smearing a fellow on behalf of a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: A master plan is an overall scheme setting out how to achieve goals over a long period.

clue.text: Little against having food first

parts.note: soup is a kind of food
as in pros and cons, con means against

explanation.surface: A small objection to eating before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for against comes first in the clue, but 'having food first' puts SOUP in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A soupçon is a very small amount or slight trace of something, a borrowing from French.

clue.text: Maybe Billy hid old trousers

indicators.note: to trouser is to pocket something, so these words keep the answer tucked inside them

parts.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: A boy named Billy concealed his old pair of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing, but it is the verb meaning pockets. Billy Idol is a British punk-era rock singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Idol is a rock singer, so his surname is an example the clue indicates with 'maybe'.

clue.text: Become weaker, and did admit saving energy

indicators.note: saving means keeping something safe inside, so the phrase holds a letter within

parts.note: taken as written
to own up is to admit
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Someone flagged and confessed to conserving their strength.
explanation.definitionFit: To die down is to lessen in intensity, as wind or noise gradually fading away.

clue.text: Loves a party followed by short sleep?

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the last letter of the word is removed

parts.note: taken as written
a do is a party or social event
a rest is a period of sleep or relaxation

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a celebration followed by a quick nap.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to be devoted to them, a strong synonym for the verb love.

clue.text: Flier heard couple getting stick, briefly

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is lopped off
heard means the word is listened to rather than read, so its sound matters

parts.note: a couple is two
a cane is a walking stick

explanation.surface: A pair being punished with a cane, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'couple' is spoken: two sounds like the first syllable of the bird's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A toucan is a tropical bird with a huge colourful beak, and a bird is something that flies.

clue.text: QI host and I leave for US city

parts.note: Sandi Toksvig hosts the BBC quiz show QI
the ego is the self, the 'I' of psychology

explanation.surface: The quiz presenter and the speaker set off on a trip to America.
explanation.walkthrough: QI is a British TV comedy quiz hosted by Sandi Toksvig since 2016; ego is Latin for I.
explanation.definitionFit: San Diego is a large city in southern California, so it is a US city.

clue.text: Trump slogan with first vowel changed will be great

indicators.note: changing the first vowel means one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: Make America Great Again, abbreviated

explanation.surface: Political commentary: tweak the Trump campaign slogan and it will be great.
explanation.walkthrough: The first A of MAGA becomes E.
explanation.definitionFit: Mega is informal slang meaning excellent or enormous, so it works as a synonym for great.

clue.text: Company manufactured a nice drug

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: something manufactured is made up from raw materials, so these letters are formed into a new word

parts.note: the letters of these two words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A firm produced a pleasant narcotic.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocaine is a stimulant narcotic made from coca leaves, so it is an illegal drug.

clue.text: Support my explanation for the audience's entertainment

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: to carry is to bear or support
my! and oh! are both exclamations of surprise
a key explains the symbols on a map or chart

explanation.surface: Someone backing their account of the evening's show to the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The three words said in a row sound like the Japanese-derived name of the pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Karaoke is singing along to recorded backing tracks, a popular form of amusement in pubs and bars.

clue.text: Some cotton on: part is annoying for neutral

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so the letters sit inside a longer stretch of text

parts.note: found running through these words

explanation.surface: Grasping a point is irritating, so remain impartial.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonpartisan person supports no political party or faction, which makes them neutral.
